content.title: About
content.content: Mashed potato with gravy is a classic restaurant side dish made from boiled potatoes that are whipped into a smooth, creamy consistency and served under a rich meat or vegetable gravy. The mash is typically enriched with butter, milk or cream, giving it a velvety texture and savory flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mashed potatoes became popular in Europe in the 17th century when milk and butter were added to improve taste.
Gravy variations—meat, mushroom, or vegetable—provide diverse flavor profiles across cuisines.
Restaurants often use high‑starch potato varieties to achieve an especially airy mash.
Mashed potatoes with gravy are commonly paired with steaks, meatballs, and baked fish.
Traditional preparation involves passing the potatoes through a sieve or press for a perfectly smooth texture.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potatoes are a good source of potassium, which supports healthy blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C source
items.content: Potatoes contain vitamin C, an antioxidant that helps strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Energy provider
items.content: The mash supplies quick‑digesting carbohydrates, useful for replenishing energy after physical activity.

items.title: Enhanced nutrient bioavailability
items.content: Cooking and mashing increase the absorption of certain vitamins and minerals.

items.title: Digestive ease
items.content: The soft texture is gentle on the stomach, making it suitable for children and those with chewing difficulties.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Butter and cream added to the mash raise its calorie count, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Gravy often contains salt; people with hypertension should opt for low‑sodium versions.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: If the gravy or mash includes milk or cream, individuals with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes have a high glycemic index, which can cause rapid spikes in blood sugar.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the mash hot as a side to meat, fish, or vegetable dishes. Garnish with fresh herbs, grated cheese, or fried onions. For a lighter version, replace cream with low‑fat milk.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep prepared mashed potatoes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. When reheating, add a splash of milk or cream to restore creaminess. Freeze only the plain mash; reheat and add gravy separately if needed.
